# The shell and plain-text files {#sec-shell}

Almost every file in this book is a **plain-text file**, and almost every tool is
run from the **shell**, the program that reads the commands you type. This chapter
covers the ideas the rest of the book takes for granted: paths, plain text
vs binary, compression (`gzip`), and joining small commands together with
pipes. If you have never used a terminal, read it slowly and type every
example yourself.

## The shell in one paragraph

When you open Terminal and `ssh` into Longleaf, you are talking to a program
called **bash**. It shows a **prompt** (something like
`[jdoe@longleaf-login1 ~]$`), waits for a line, runs it, prints the result,
and shows the prompt again. A command is a program name followed by
**arguments**, separated by spaces:

```bash
ls   -l   -h   /proj/phanstiel_lab
#^   ^^^^^^^   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
#program options  argument (what to act on)
```

Options that start with one dash are short (`-h`); two dashes are long
(`--help`). Almost every tool prints its own manual with `--help` or
`man <tool>`.

## Files, folders and paths

Everything lives in one tree that starts at `/` (the **root**).

```
/
├── nas/longleaf/home/jdoe/        <- your home, also called ~
├── proj/phanstiel_lab/
│   ├── Data/
│   └── Reference/human/hg38/
└── work/users/j/d/jdoe/
```

- An **absolute path** starts at `/` and works from anywhere:
  `/proj/phanstiel_lab/Reference/human/hg38/`.
- A **relative path** starts from where you are now (`pwd`):
  `output/align/sample_sorted.bam`. bagPipes uses relative paths, which
  is why you must `cd` into the bagPipes folder before running it.
- `.` means "this folder", `..` means "the folder above", `~` means "my home".

::: {.callout-warning}
## Spaces and odd characters in names

The shell splits on spaces, so `my file.txt` looks like two arguments.
Use only letters, numbers, `_`, `-` and `.` in file and sample names. This
matters for bagPipes too, because sample names become file names.
:::

## Plain text vs binary

A **plain-text** file is a sequence of readable characters. You can open
it with `less`, `head` or any text editor and understand it. FASTQ, FASTA,
GTF, BED, SAM, the samplesheet and the config file are all plain text.

A **binary** file stores numbers in a compact form meant for programs,
not people. If you `cat` one, you get garbage. BAM, bigWig and RDS files are
binary; each has a tool that turns it back into text (`samtools view`,
`bigWigToBedGraph`, `readRDS()` in R).

```bash
head -4 RNAsamplesheet.txt        # readable
head -c 200 sample_sorted.bam     # garbage: it is binary (and compressed)
file sample_sorted.bam            # `file` guesses what a file is
```

### Tab-separated tables

Most genomics text files are **tables**: one record per line, columns
separated by a **tab** character (TSV). Tabs and spaces look the same on
screen but they're different characters, and tools that expect tabs will
break on spaces. To see the tabs:

```bash
cat -A RNAsamplesheet.txt | head -2   # tabs show as ^I, line ends as $
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Excel and Windows line endings

Saving a samplesheet from Excel can add Windows line endings (`^M$` in `cat -A`)
or turn `00h` into a date. Check with `cat -A` after you edit a table in Excel.
:::

## Compression and gzip

Sequencing files are huge: one sample can be tens of gigabytes as plain
text. FASTQ text repeats the same few letters (`A`, `C`, `G`, `T`) over and over,
so it **compresses** very well. **gzip** is the standard compression
program, and files compressed with it end in `.gz`. A compressed FASTQ is
typically 3–5 times smaller.

```bash
gzip reads.fastq            # compress   -> reads.fastq.gz  (original removed)
gunzip reads.fastq.gz       # decompress -> reads.fastq     (original removed)
gzip -c reads.fastq > reads.fastq.gz   # -c: write to the screen/redirect, keep original
```

You almost never need to decompress. The tools in this book (FastQC, Trim
Galore, Salmon, HISAT2) read `.fastq.gz` directly, and you can *look* inside
without unpacking:

```bash
zcat reads.fastq.gz | head -8      # print the first 8 lines (2 reads)
zless reads.fastq.gz               # page through it (q to quit)
zgrep -c "^@" reads.fastq.gz       # rough read count (header lines; see note)
gzip -t reads.fastq.gz && echo OK  # test the file isn't corrupted
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why `zgrep -c "^@"` is only rough

Quality strings can also start with `@`, so this can over-count. Counting
lines and dividing by four is the reliable way:
`echo $(( $(zcat reads.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))`.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## gzip vs bgzip

**bgzip** (from the htslib/samtools family) writes a special kind of gzip in
independent blocks. It is still readable by `zcat`, but programs can also jump
to the middle of it, which is what makes indexed files (BAM, `.vcf.gz` +
`.tbi`, `.bed.gz` + `.tbi`) possible. BAM files are bgzip-compressed
internally. For FASTQ, plain `gzip` is fine.
:::

## Checksums: did the file copy correctly?

A **checksum** is a short fingerprint of a file's contents. If even one
byte changes, the fingerprint changes. Sequencing cores and public
databases publish MD5 checksums so you can check your download.

```bash
md5sum sample_R1_001.fastq.gz
# 3b5d5c3712955042212316173ccf37be  sample_R1_001.fastq.gz
md5sum -c md5sums.txt     # check every file listed in a checksum file
```

## Standard output, standard error and redirection

Every program has two output streams:

- **standard output (stdout, stream 1):** the results.
- **standard error (stderr, stream 2):** messages, progress, warnings and errors.

Both print to the screen by default. You can **redirect** them into files:

```bash
fastqc reads.fastq.gz > fastqc.out           # stdout to a file (overwrite)
fastqc reads.fastq.gz >> fastqc.out          # append instead
fastqc reads.fastq.gz 1> fastqc.out 2> fastqc.err   # each stream to its own file
```

This is exactly what every bagPipes rule does, so you'll see a matching
`.out` / `.err` pair for each step in `output/logs/`:

```
fastqc -o output/QC R1.fastq.gz R2.fastq.gz 1> output/logs/fastqc_{sample}.out 2> output/logs/fastqc_{sample}.err
```

Many tools write their **useful summary to stderr** (Trim Galore, HISAT2
and Salmon all do), so when you're looking for "how did it go?", check the
`.err` file first.

## Pipes: joining small tools together

The pipe `|` sends the stdout of one command into the next, without
writing a file in between. This is the most important idea in the Unix
shell: small tools that each do one thing, joined together.

```bash
zcat reads.fastq.gz | head -4000 | wc -l
# decompress -> keep the first 4000 lines -> count them  => 4000
```

The bagPipes `align` rule is a pipe: HISAT2 writes alignments to stdout,
`samtools view` converts them to BAM, and `samtools sort` sorts them and
writes the file. Nothing is written to disk until the end.

```bash
hisat2 -x index -1 R1.fq.gz -2 R2.fq.gz | samtools view -u | samtools sort -o out.bam
```

## The everyday toolkit

| Command | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `head`, `tail` | First / last lines | `head -n 20 quant.sf` |
| `less` | Scroll through a file (`/` to search, `q` to quit) | `less -S file.gtf` (`-S`: don't wrap long lines) |
| `wc -l` | Count lines | `wc -l genes.bed` |
| `grep` | Keep lines matching a pattern | `grep -w "GAPDH" genes.gtf` |
| `cut` | Keep certain columns | `cut -f1,4,5 genes.gtf` |
| `sort` | Sort lines | `sort -k4,4gr quant.sf` (column 4, numeric, reverse) |
| `uniq -c` | Count identical neighbouring lines (sort first) | `cut -f3 genes.gtf \| sort \| uniq -c` |
| `awk` | Filter and compute on columns | `awk '$5 > 100' quant.sf` (NumReads > 100) |
| `column -t` | Line up columns for reading | `head quant.sf \| column -t` |
| `ls -lh`, `du -sh` | File and folder sizes | `du -sh output/*` |

### A worked example: what feature types are in a GTF?

```bash
GTF=/proj/phanstiel_lab/Reference/human/hg38/annotations/gencode.v49.primary_assembly.annotation.gtf
grep -v "^#" $GTF | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr
```

Read it left to right: drop comment lines → keep column 3 (the feature
type) → sort → count each distinct value → sort by count. You'll see
lines like `exon`, `CDS`, `UTR`, `transcript`, `gene`, each with a count.

## Variables, wildcards and loops

```bash
D=/proj/phanstiel_lab/Data/processed/subsamples/rna/PE_100k/subsampled   # a variable
ls $D                        # use it with $
ls $D/*_R1_001.fastq.gz      # * matches anything: all R1 files

# do something to every file
for f in $D/*_R1_001.fastq.gz; do
  echo "$(basename $f): $(( $(zcat $f | wc -l) / 4 )) reads"
done
```

`basename` strips the folder from a path; bagPipes uses it to rename
outputs (`$(basename {input.R1} .fastq.gz)` also strips the ending).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. You run `trim_galore ... 1> trim.out 2> trim.err` and want to see how many
   reads had adapters. Which file do you open?
2. Why is `zcat reads.fastq.gz | head` much faster than
   `gunzip reads.fastq.gz; head reads.fastq`?
3. What does `cut -f1 quant.sf | grep -c ENST` print?
4. Your samplesheet looks fine in a text editor but bagPipes says the column
   `Read1` doesn't exist. What would you check?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Answers

1. `trim.err` probably. Trim Galore writes its progress and summary to stderr.
   (It also writes a `_trimming_report.txt`.)
2. `head` stops reading after 10 lines, and `zcat` stops when nothing is reading
   from the pipe any more. `gunzip` decompresses the whole file to disk first.
3. The number of lines whose first column contains `ENST`: the number of
   transcripts in the file.
4. Whether the columns are separated by tabs (`cat -A` shows `^I`), and whether
   the header has stray spaces or Windows line endings (`^M`).
:::
:::
